dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core framing of Harvey as potential workflow and professional-services infrastructure, then materially develops it through a five-ring platform-and-ecosystem model. It also sharpens the cluster’s central uncertainty: ecosystem expansion, commercial traction and institutional purchasing do not establish sustained everyday use or defensibility against foundation-model platforms.
qs: It's whether Harvey is building the infrastructure through which AI-powered professional services are delivered — with law firms as a central node in the distribution channel.
You can't govern an ecosystem people aren't actively using — and the adoption gap remains real.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central claim that AI efficiency threatens the billable-hour pyramid by automating junior technical work that subsidises senior judgment. It materially extends the synthesis by identifying Harvey’s revenue-sharing and co-built workflow experiments as a concrete attempt to help firms commercialise AI-enabled outputs, although it does not address the associated training pipeline in depth.
qs: If AI hollows out the base, the economics of the whole structure are threatened.

It has begun experimenting with a different revenue structure entirely — moving from seat-based software pricing to revenue-share arrangements where Harvey co-builds AI-powered workflows with law firms, and those firms commercialise the output for their clients.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI adoption is a business-model problem, directly linking efficiency to hourly-billing conflict and pressure on pyramidal staffing. It materially extends the synthesis by presenting Harvey’s shared infrastructure and revenue-sharing workflows as a concrete, though explicitly unproven, route toward different services and pricing.
qs: Law firms bill by the hour, and Harvey makes them faster — which means, in the short term, AI efficiency doesn't obviously help the business model.

It has begun experimenting with a different revenue structure entirely — moving from seat-based software pricing to revenue-share arrangements where Harvey co-builds AI-powered workflows with law firms, and those firms commercialise the output for their clients.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s view that competitive advantage may shift toward differentiated, client-integrated delivery architectures and materially extends it by proposing Harvey as infrastructure through which law firms could distribute AI-powered professional services. Shared Spaces provides a concrete platform example, although the claimed structural benefits remain speculative rather than demonstrated.
qs: It's whether Harvey is building the infrastructure through which AI-powered professional services are delivered — with law firms as a central node in the distribution channel.
Could legal tech get law firms and their corporate clients working together in one system?

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI chiefly disrupts legal production, hourly billing and pyramid economics rather than eliminating high-value legal judgment. It materially extends the cluster by presenting Harvey’s revenue-sharing workflows and shared platform as a concrete model in which law firms become distribution nodes for broader AI-enabled professional services, while acknowledging that scalability remains unproven.
qs: Law firms bill by the hour, and Harvey makes them faster — which means, in the short term, AI efficiency doesn't obviously help the business model.
It's whether Harvey is building the infrastructure through which AI-powered professional services are delivered — with law firms as a central node in the distribution channel.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source extends the cluster’s proposition with a concrete platform-distribution model: Harvey could supply shared infrastructure through which law firms and corporate clients coordinate AI-powered professional services. It directly develops the cluster’s questions about shifting market boundaries and value capture, while treating structural gains for law firms and adoption outcomes as unresolved.
qs: It's whether Harvey is building the infrastructure through which AI-powered professional services are delivered — with law firms as a central node in the distribution channel.
If so, does just Harvey benefit, or do law and legal firms structurally benefit too?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that value comes from redesigning work and organisational systems rather than merely adding an AI assistant, then materially extends the cluster by describing Harvey as matter-centric infrastructure for encoded workflows, cross-organisational collaboration and multidisciplinary services. Its cautions about limited routine use, scalability and defensibility align with the cluster’s distinction between adoption and realised value.
qs: Their Workflow Builder let firms encode proprietary knowledge into structured, repeatable processes.
It's a feature for doing different work entirely — integrated, multi-disciplinary, with law as the coordinating node.

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: The source accepts that trust and adoption depend on workflow integration and organisational behaviour, not error-free performance alone. It materially extends the cluster by proposing professional-identity threat as a two-sided barrier and by describing engagement as bimodal: low use among most licence holders but deep use after a multi-product integration threshold. It does not directly establish verification costs or evaluate specific safeguards.
qs: That creates a double bind with AI: if the tool isn't reliable enough, it makes mistakes, and lawyers don't trust it.
It's a sharp split: most lawyers barely touch the tool, but those who cross some threshold of integration become deeply embedded in it.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: The source aligns closely with the synthesis: it treats Harvey’s elite-firm incubation, security and governance investments, matter-centric workflows, and custom agents as evidence of an enterprise platform strategy rather than a mere chatbot. It also preserves the synthesis’s evidentiary limits by declining to validate product quality and leaving workflow lock-in and long-term defensibility unresolved.
qs: This sort of acceptance by a major law firm was an enormous boost to the credibility of this fledgling startup.
This was an ecosystem and platform play that went beyond a narrow AI tool story.

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of a contested supplier–partner–rival market. It presents Harvey and Legora as competing legal-AI platforms while identifying direct foundation-model partnerships as a credible bypass route for capable firms, and it reinforces the distinction between licence adoption and actual use. It leaves platform dominance unresolved rather than claiming realised displacement.
qs: For firms with the internal capability to do their own AI engineering, the intermediation layer is increasingly optional.
Adoption in terms of licences is reportedly high; actual use remains relatively low.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s distinction between purchasing, engagement and effective use. It argues that broad licensing has not produced broadly transformative use-level product-market fit, while identifying a deeply engaged minority and workflow integration—not aggregate adoption—as the more meaningful indicators. Its platform and economic analysis adds context but does not materially redirect the cluster’s proposition.
qs: One word of caution: adoption in terms of licenses is reportedly high, but actual use apparently remains relatively low.

Harvey hasn't yet created the kind of pull where the tool reshapes how you work rather than slotting into how you already work — the kind of pull that is an unmistakeable sign of product-market fit at the use level rather than the purchasing level.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified proposition: it interprets Harvey’s workflow, governance and ecosystem strategy as a credible route to becoming legal-services infrastructure, while explicitly declining to infer durable defensibility or usage-level product-market fit from enterprise reach and commercial traction.
qs: Both arguments have force, and the second of them — the question of whether vertical legal AI can hold its position as the underlying foundation models become more capable and more direct in their pursuit of the legal market — is one we genuinely don't know the answer to.
You can't govern an ecosystem people aren't actively using — and the adoption gap remains real.

kp.k: Strategic interpretation is not a product evaluation
kp.d: Roberts and Wilkins reject the framing of Harvey as merely an overvalued ChatGPT wrapper, interpreting its development as overlapping moves from assistant to governance, platform, infrastructure and ecosystem coordination. They explicitly have not tried the product and cannot vouch for its performance; enterprise-only access limits outsiders' understanding.
qs: Neither of us has tried Harvey, so we can't vouch for it as a product.
Harvey's evolution is better captured as concentric circles than as sequential pivots. Each phase builds on and incorporates the previous one.

kp.k: Breadth and firm incubation underpinned early adoption
kp.d: The authors report that Harvey's founders favored a broad conversational legal assistant over narrow task automation after early GPT-4 access. Allen & Overy provided experimentation inside the firm, senior sponsorship and an enterprise-wide rollout to 3,500 attorneys, giving Harvey credibility and early exposure to implementation difficulties.
qs: A conversational AI associate that could do many things rather than one thing perfectly.
A&O rolled Harvey out to 3,500 attorneys through a top-down, enterprise-wide deal.
It was a true incubation, not just a vendor relationship.

kp.k: Governance and security become competitive advantages
kp.d: The authors interpret Harvey's investment in isolated environments, administrative controls, firm-system integration and matter separation as a mechanism for winning enterprise trust, rather than simply meeting compliance obligations. The claim concerns market positioning, not independently tested security performance.
qs: What they realized was that governance wasn't just a compliance burden. In legal, it's a competitive lever.
Security infrastructure, isolated computing environments, admin controls, links to firm systems, separation of client matters.

kp.k: Custom workflows turn users into platform builders
kp.d: Matter-centric workspaces and Workflow Builder allow firms to encode proprietary knowledge into repeatable processes. The essay reports 18,000+ custom workflows and 25,000+ custom agents, interpreting customization as increased ownership and platform development, while explicitly withholding conclusions about portability and lock-in.
qs: The numbers are striking: 18,000+ custom workflows, 25,000+ custom agents.
Firms weren't just using Harvey. They were building on it.
Users feel much more ownership over AI tools they build and customize, though we don't know how portable these workflows would be off Harvey, so we don't know how sticky they are.

kp.k: Shared Spaces connects firms, clients and consulting advisers
kp.d: The essay reports that December 2025's Shared Spaces lets firms invite even noncustomer clients into common AI workspaces. PwC and IFS participated alongside firms on M&A analysis, while Gleiss Lutz and Deutsche Telekom collaborated on regulation. The authors interpret this as positioning toward coordination infrastructure for multidisciplinary matters, not proof that this role has been secured.
qs: In December 2025, Harvey launched Shared Spaces — a feature that lets law firms and their clients work in the same AI-powered workspace.
Guest accounts mean firms can invite clients who aren't Harvey customers.
Harvey is positioning to become the infrastructure layer that coordinates complex deals and all the players involved in them.

kp.k: Acquisitions and investments extend ecosystem ambitions
kp.d: The authors interpret Harvey's early-2026 acquisition of Hexus as engineering-capability acquisition and its partnership with The LegalTech Fund as ecosystem shaping. The fund is described as a $110 million venture firm backed by McDermott and Orrick; co-investments of up to $2 million per startup target complementary point solutions. Weinberg's marketplace framing supports the authors' interpretation, rather than demonstrating achieved ecosystem control.
qs: It bought Hexus, a startup that builds AI-powered product demos and guides — not a legal AI company, but an engineering talent play.
Up to $2 million per startup, focused on "point solution providers" — complementary tools, not competitors.
It's about shaping who else builds, what gets built, and how capital flows through the legal technology landscape.

kp.d: Harvey's Claude Marketplace participation, Model Context Protocol integration and use of OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are presented as a strategy of meeting users inside their chosen foundation-model environment. The authors contrast this with LexisNexis absorbing Claude into Protégé, and explicitly leave unresolved whether foundation-model companies will capture legal workflows and customer relationships themselves.
qs: Harvey chose to be complementary middleware — going to where the users are rather than pulling users to itself.
Harvey also moved to a multi-model strategy — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google — becoming model-agnostic rather than tied to any single foundation model.

The counter-bet — held by some of the dismissers from the section above — is that the foundation model companies themselves will move into the customer relationship and the legal-specific workflows, leaving Harvey squeezed from above as well as from below.

kp.k: Law firms could distribute AI across professional services
kp.d: The authors hypothesize that lawyers' involvement across business decisions makes firms potential distribution nodes for AI-enabled professional services. They report Harvey's $11 billion valuation as roughly ten times the largest accounting AI company and claim no standalone consulting AI company has meaningful scale. Drawing on Marc Andrusko's accounting-software analogy, they ask whether shared infrastructure could benefit law's structural position as well as Harvey; this remains a strategic possibility.
qs: QuickBooks and similar products benefited enormously from accountants acting as distribution nodes — a small business and its external CPA sharing the same file, using the same tools.
What if law firms are not a beachhead for AI in the legal industry? What if they are a beachhead for professional services more generally?
If so, does just Harvey benefit, or do law and legal firms structurally benefit too?

kp.k: Licence adoption does not establish sustained usage
kp.d: The authors distinguish reported high licence adoption from apparently low actual use, citing a16z's acknowledgment of limited engagement. They argue that Harvey has not yet clearly demonstrated usage-level product-market fit that changes working practices, while acknowledging that their perspective does not include direct product experience.
qs: One word of caution: adoption in terms of licenses is reportedly high, but actual use apparently remains relatively low.
a16z's own analysis acknowledged that Harvey is "there and available" at major firms but "not heavily used yet."

Harvey hasn't yet created the kind of pull where the tool reshapes how you work rather than slotting into how you already work — the kind of pull that is an unmistakeable sign of product-market fit at the use level rather than the purchasing level.

kp.k: Identity threat may reinforce resistance to AI
kp.d: Beyond technological conservatism, the authors propose that junior and mid-level lawyers may identify their professional value with reading and reproducing technical legal information. They describe a double bind: unreliable AI provokes distrust, while reliable AI provokes fear of substitution. This is an explanatory hypothesis, not a measured finding.
qs: But the deeper reason may be an identity threat.

That creates a double bind with AI: if the tool isn't reliable enough, it makes mistakes, and lawyers don't trust it. If the tool is too reliable, it threatens to put them out of business, and lawyers are afraid of it.

kp.k: Vendor data suggests sharply uneven user engagement
kp.d: Harvey's own data reportedly places daily active usage at 75-85 percent among users adopting four or more product lines; the essay provides no sample size or measurement period. The authors interpret this selected-group statistic alongside low broader engagement as bimodal adoption and suggest that power users working with AI as a cognitive partner may reveal future professional practices.
qs: Harvey's own data indicates that for users who have adopted four or more product lines, daily active usage runs at 75-85 percent
It's a sharp split: most lawyers barely touch the tool, but those who cross some threshold of integration become deeply embedded in it.

kp.k: Automation threatens hourly economics and the staffing pyramid
kp.d: The authors argue that faster work does not obviously benefit hourly-billing firms in the short term. They describe junior technical work at the pyramid's base as subsidizing senior judgment and client relationships, assert that this technical work is already being automated, and predict a threat to firm economics if automation hollows out the base.
qs: Law firms bill by the hour, and Harvey makes them faster — which means, in the short term, AI efficiency doesn't obviously help the business model.
The base subsidises the apex — that's how firms make money. AI is automating the base.
If AI hollows out the base, the economics of the whole structure are threatened.

kp.k: Revenue sharing experiments recast software as service infrastructure
kp.d: The essay reports Harvey experimenting beyond seat-based pricing through revenue-sharing arrangements in which it co-builds workflows that firms commercialize for clients. The authors suggest this could turn Harvey into a channel for selling different services and accessing professional-services budgets, partially addressing the hourly-billing paradox; scalability beyond sophisticated firms remains uncertain.
qs: moving from seat-based software pricing to revenue-share arrangements where Harvey co-builds AI-powered workflows with law firms, and those firms commercialise the output for their clients.
If it works, it's a partial answer to the billing paradox: not faster hours, but different work sold differently.
But it's early, and whether this model scales beyond a handful of sophisticated firms remains to be seen.

kp.k: Infrastructure could enable fundamentally different professional work
kp.d: The authors distinguish three technological pathways: cheaper and faster existing work, demand expansion through lower costs, and fundamentally different work. They place most lawyers on the first path and interpret Harvey's outer rings as enabling the third: integrated multidisciplinary services coordinated through law, with ecosystem governance potentially shaping the tools available for that work.
qs: three paths that technology creates for any profession: doing the same thing cheaper and faster, expanding demand through lower costs, or doing fundamentally different things.
It's a feature for doing different work entirely — integrated, multi-disciplinary, with law as the coordinating node.

kp.k: Ecosystem expansion may mask unresolved product-market fit
kp.d: The authors offer a competing interpretation of Harvey's escalation: moving into capital allocation and marketplace coordination may be easier than changing lawyers' daily practices. They make successful ecosystem governance conditional on thriving underlying usage and leave open whether outer-ring expansion can succeed while core capabilities remain underused.
qs: You can't govern an ecosystem people aren't actively using — and the adoption gap remains real.

From another, it looks like the classic pattern of a technology company moving upmarket — retreating from the hard, unresolved problem of product-market fit at the usage level into the structurally easier work of capital allocation and marketplace orchestration.

kp.k: May launches expand agents and benchmark governance
kp.d: The May update reports Harvey's 5 May 2026 launch of 500-plus legal agents, a plain-English Agent Builder and Legal Agent Bench: 1,200-plus tasks across 24 practice areas with 75,000-plus expert-written rubric criteria. Named collaborators include foundation-model companies, Nvidia and other technical organizations. The authors see defining benchmark standards as strengthening ecosystem governance; no benchmark performance results are given. Harvey also disclosed more than 100,000 lawyers across 1,500 organisations.
qs: a public benchmark called Legal Agent Bench (LAB) — 1,200-plus tasks across 24 practice areas, evaluated by 75,000-plus expert-written rubric criteria.
Owning the benchmark is a classic ecosystem-governor move — whoever defines what "good" looks like in the category shapes what everyone else builds toward.
Harvey also disclosed an updated user base of more than 100,000 lawyers across 1,500 organisations.

kp.k: Firmwide deployments coexist with substantial platform rivalry
kp.d: The update reports Slaughter and May's firmwide Harvey deployment on 29 April 2026 as further elite-firm validation. It also reports Legora's $5.6 billion valuation on 30 April 2026, Nvidia investment through NVentures and more than $100 million ARR, with some customers also using Harvey. The authors interpret these developments as evidence for an emerging top-end duopoly rather than single-platform dominance.
qs: Slaughter and May went firmwide with Harvey on 29 April 2026.
Legora reached a $5.6 billion valuation on 30 April 2026,
Legora has crossed $100 million in ARR
the category is forming into something more like a duopoly at the top than a single dominant platform.

kp.k: Direct foundation-model partnerships threaten vertical intermediation
kp.d: The update reports Freshfields' 23 April 2026 multiyear Anthropic partnership covering 5,700 employees and co-development of legal applications, alongside Claude for Word's 11 April beta. It also reports Anthropic's $1.5 billion services joint venture and OpenAI's parallel $10 billion services venture on 4 May. The authors interpret these as concrete competitive pressure: firms with internal AI-engineering capability increasingly may bypass vertical legal-AI vendors, although Harvey's eventual outcome remains unresolved.
qs: Freshfields signed a multi-year direct partnership with Anthropic on 23 April 2026,
deploying Claude across 5,700 employees and entering a co-development program to build legal-focused AI applications.
For firms with the internal capability to do their own AI engineering, the intermediation layer is increasingly optional.
Whether Harvey's infrastructure-and-ecosystem play continues to compound or whether the bigger firms route around it is now one of the live questions in the category.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Roberts and Wilkins interpret Harvey as an emerging infrastructure and ecosystem business that could reorganize professional-services delivery around law firms, while identifying unresolved adoption, business-model and competitive constraints.
pts.d: The authors make nine linked claims. (1) Harvey's development comprises five cumulative layers: a broad legal assistant, enterprise governance and security, a customizable platform, shared professional-services infrastructure, and ecosystem governance. They argue that governance is a competitive advantage in legal markets, not merely a compliance requirement. Custom workflows and agents turn firms into builders on the platform, although their portability and resulting customer stickiness are unknown. (2) Shared Spaces could make law firms coordinating and distribution nodes for integrated work involving corporate clients and consulting advisers. This is a conditional prediction about doing different, multidisciplinary work, not just accelerating existing legal tasks; whether law firms themselves capture structural benefits remains an open question. (3) Acquisitions, complementary startup investments, marketplace integration and Harvey's own Legal Agent Bench are interpreted as moves to influence what others build and how capital flows through legal technology. The authors argue that defining benchmark standards can shape development across the category. (4) Harvey's multi-model middleware strategy bets that enterprises will standardize on foundation models and invoke specialized legal workflows within them. However, foundation-model companies' direct legal applications, firm partnerships and services ventures could make this intermediary optional, particularly for firms with internal AI-engineering capability. (5) The authors anticipate two or three major legal-AI platforms rather than a single winner; their May update interprets Legora's growth as movement toward a duopoly at the top. (6) License purchases do not necessarily produce routine use or usage-level product-market fit. Adoption may be bimodal: many lawyers use Harvey little, while deeply integrated users use it intensively. The authors suggest, rather than establish, that professional identity threat contributes to resistance: unreliable AI is distrusted, while reliable AI threatens lawyers whose professional identity rests on technical document work. (7) They assert that AI is already automating junior-level technical work and will increasingly threaten the pyramid economics in which the base subsidizes senior judgment and client relationships. Faster work also conflicts with hourly billing in the short term. (8) They describe Harvey's experiments with co-built workflows and revenue-sharing as a possible partial solution: firms would commercialize AI-enabled services rather than merely buy software to perform existing work faster. They say this accesses a much larger professional-services budget, but scalability remains unresolved. (9) They distinguish cheaper and faster existing work, demand expansion through lower costs, and fundamentally different work. Most lawyers are said to remain on the first path, while Harvey's outer layers are positioned for the third. They also offer an alternative interpretation: ecosystem expansion could be a retreat from the harder problem of changing lawyers' daily working practices, rather than proof that the underlying product has achieved deep adoption.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The analysis rests on reported company developments, adoption figures, partnerships and market events, supplemented by the authors' professional perspectives; it does not offer firsthand product testing or measured effects on legal-service outcomes.
pts.d: Roberts and Wilkins explicitly say neither has tried Harvey. Roberts contributes experience building and orchestrating AI agents and observing adoption; Wilkins contributes a historical perspective on legal-services organization. The five-layer interpretation draws on A&O's reported rollout to 3,500 attorneys; enterprise security and matter-centric architecture; more than 18,000 custom workflows and 25,000 custom agents; Shared Spaces collaborations involving PwC and IFS on M&A and Gleiss Lutz and Deutsche Telekom on regulatory matters; the Hexus acquisition; Claude Marketplace and Model Context Protocol integration; support for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google models; and co-investment with The LegalTech Fund of up to $2 million per startup. Their wider professional-services positioning argument cites Harvey's $11 billion valuation, asserted to be about ten times that of the largest accounting-AI company, and an asserted absence of a standalone consulting-AI company at meaningful scale. These are market-position indicators, not demonstrations of productivity or service quality. For adoption, they cite a16z's characterization of limited use and Harvey's own reported 75–85 percent daily active usage among users adopting at least four product lines. No denominator definition, independent validation or causal analysis is supplied for that usage statistic. The identity-threat explanation is an interpretive hypothesis; no systematic study is presented. Likewise, the discussion of pyramid economics and revenue sharing offers a mechanism and reported experimentation, not measured employment, profitability or client-price effects. The May update adds a reported library of over 500 agents, an Agent Builder, and Harvey's Legal Agent Bench: over 1,200 tasks across 24 practice areas with over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria and named technology partners. The essay uses LAB's creation and partnerships as evidence of ecosystem positioning, not as a reported agent-performance result. It also cites Harvey's disclosed user base of over 100,000 lawyers across 1,500 organizations, Slaughter and May's firmwide adoption, Legora's $5.6 billion valuation and over $100 million ARR, Freshfields' direct Anthropic partnership covering 5,700 employees, Claude for Word, and announced Anthropic and OpenAI services ventures. These developments are treated as strategic pressure tests, not conclusive proof of the predicted market structure.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The essay analyzes developments through May 2026, predicts accelerating technical automation without a precise deadline, and makes longer-term infrastructure outcomes conditional on actual use, firm capabilities and competitive developments.
pts.d: The authors drafted the essay at the end of March 2026 and updated it in May. Shared Spaces is dated to December 2025; acquisitions and ecosystem expansion to early 2026. The update dates Freshfields' Anthropic agreement to 23 April, Slaughter and May's rollout to 29 April, Legora's valuation to 30 April, the foundation-model companies' services-venture announcements to 4 May, and Harvey's agents and LAB launch to 5 May. Junior technical-work automation is presented as already occurring and expected to accelerate as tools become faster, more widely used and more accepted; no displacement magnitude or fixed deadline is given. The hourly-billing conflict is expressly short-term. Revenue sharing is early-stage and conditional on expansion beyond a handful of sophisticated firms. Workflow portability and customer lock-in are explicitly unknown. The middleware strategy depends on enterprise adoption of foundation-model interfaces while specialized workflows retain value; direct model-company relationships are especially viable for firms able to engineer their own applications. The proposed ecosystem-governance role requires thriving inner layers and sustained active use. Whether outer-layer expansion can succeed despite underutilization is framed as a question for the next few years. The authors do not claim that law firms necessarily benefit from Harvey's success or that a dominant vertical intermediary will survive. The May update strengthens their interpretation of Harvey's ecosystem ambitions while increasing uncertainty about competitive concentration and disintermediation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are enterprise law firms, junior and mid-level lawyers, sophisticated corporate clients, consulting advisers, and competing or complementary AI businesses.
pts.d: Elite and large law firms are the central setting: they may gain trusted AI infrastructure, encode proprietary knowledge, distribute AI-enabled services to clients and coordinate multidisciplinary engagements, while facing reduced hourly revenue, pressure on junior-work economics and possible platform dependence. Junior lawyers are particularly exposed to automation of the technical work at the pyramid's base; junior to mid-level lawyers are also identified as susceptible to identity-based resistance. Senior and elite lawyers' judgment, relationships and cross-domain coordination are positioned as potentially more central, although the authors question whether firms capture the resulting benefits. Power users may move toward the authors' proposed 'cyborg lawyer' model, working with AI as a cognitive partner rather than simply using it for isolated tasks. Corporate legal-service buyers and their advisers could collaborate in shared matter workspaces, including through guest access without separate Harvey subscriptions. Consulting firms, including PwC in the example, participate alongside law firms and corporate clients rather than being conflated with software vendors. Harvey and Legora compete for platform positions; complementary legal-tech startups may receive investment and distribution opportunities while becoming subject to platform-defined standards. Foundation-model companies compete with, supply and distribute vertical platforms, and increasingly pursue direct customer relationships and services delivery. Firms with strong internal engineering capabilities may bypass vertical vendors. The document does not offer a concrete prediction about access to justice, unmet individual civil legal needs or small-firm outcomes.
